title: The bedtime Shema
hookLine: before sleep: the Shema, and forgiveness for anyone who hurt you that day

cards: Late at night, lights off. A tired body, a mind replaying the day. What she said in the meeting.
The text he never answered. The driver who cut in. The comeback, rewritten.
Midnight, then one. A grudge makes a strange pillow, and plenty of nights end on one. Jewish tradition has a practice for this hour, and its first step is letting go.
Today: Modeh Ani, and its bookend.

teach.b: Back in camp one, you learned the Shema, the line at the heart of Jewish prayer. In the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one."
The Torah says to speak these words "when thou liest down, and when thou risest up." Jews say the Shema in the evening prayers, and the Talmud says to say it again in bed, right before sleep.
It points to a psalm: "commune with your own heart upon your bed, and be still." Over the centuries, it grew into a short bedtime service.

teach.h: I FORGIVE ANYONE WHO HURT ME.
teach.b: Many prayer books begin with a declaration: first, a person forgives anyone who angered or hurt them that day, in body, money, honor or anything else, by accident or on purpose, and asks that no one be punished on their account.
The Talmud tells of Mar Zutra, a rabbi who did this every night: before bed, he said, I forgive everyone who troubled me. Then the Shema, and a blessing thanking God, who lets sleep fall on my eyes.
Many add a psalm: "Into Thy hand I commit my spirit."
And in many homes, children and adults say a line about four angels: Michael on my right, Gabriel on my left, Uriel in front, Raphael behind, and above my head, God's presence.
Angels came up before, in the Friday-night song of welcome; at bedtime, four are named. See the shape of it.

teach.h: INTO THY HAND I COMMIT MY SPIRIT.
teach.b: It opens with thank you, Modeh Ani, before your feet touch the floor. It closes with I forgive you, before your eyes close. Blessings all the way through.

how: Before sleep, many Jews say the bedtime Shema: a declaration forgiving anyone who wronged them, the Shema, the Hamapil blessing, and verses such as Psalm 31:6 and the line about the four angels.

o: a blessing said before eating breakfast
thanks said on waking, before you get up
a bedtime prayer asking God to forgive you

games.q: what's inside the bedtime Shema — tap the pairs.
p: why the Shema is said at night
on my right, on my left

s: the bedtime Shema begins by forgiving others
many prayer books open it with forgiving anyone who hurt you that day.
forgiving at bedtime means saying the other person was right
it means setting the hurt down and asking that no one be punished on your account.
the Shema is said only in the morning
"when thou liest down, and when thou risest up": morning, evening, and again in bed.

games.q: you're in bed. the day went badly, and someone hurt you. the bedtime Shema is next. what comes first, in many prayer books?
games.why: it opens by forgiving anyone who angered or hurt you, like Mar Zutra, who forgave everyone who troubled him before bed.

practice: Let one small hurt from today or this week come to mind, not the biggest, something you can manage, and picture the person.

You don't have to say they were right, or call them; set it down, the way you'd put a heavy bag on the floor before bed, and say to yourself: I forgive this, for tonight. If you pray, you can hand it to God.

wordCard.voice: Modeh Ani, the morning thanks said before your feet touch the floor, the bookend to the bedtime Shema's forgiveness before sleep.

orig.note: Hebrew: the reading of the Shema upon the bed.

carryVoice: Your line: forgive before sleeping. Tomorrow a new part begins: the holidays, starting with the calendar. Day one hundred twenty, and counting.
